China’s export controls fragment rare earths market – Argus Metals

## China’s export controls fragment rare earths market 

### Published date: 06 May 2025

China's export controls on certain rare earths have sent shockwaves around the global market since 4 April, fragmenting it into several increasingly distinct pricing regions — China, the US, Europe and beyond.

The first half of April was characterised by soaring bids for the restricted products outside China, but reticence to sell from those with any material held outside China. Availability of the restricted rare earths — dysprosium, terbium, gadolinium, yttrium, samarium, lutetium and scandium — is tight outside China and traders have been wary of selling in case they struggle to restock. It can be particularly difficult for traders to secure critical mineral export licences from China because of the level of detail required about end-users and applications.

But spot deals emerged in the second half of April in the Atlantic basin and pockets of Asia at much higher prices than fob China indexes, which have hardly moved owing to the sudden halt in exports. Spot deals have largely focused on yttrium and gadolinium products so far, with dysprosium and terbium widely discussed but actual trades scarce.

Argus' monthly European price assessments for the restricted rare earths jumped sharply on 1 May, reflecting this combination of spot deals, bids and offers.

Dysprosium oxide rose to $700-1,000/kg cif Europe on 1 May, which compares with Argus' fob China index of $240-245/kg on the same day. The terbium oxide assessment rose to $2,000-4,000/kg cif Europe on 1 May, compared with the fob China index at $990-1,010/kg on the same day. Some offers were heard for both terbium and dysprosium oxide at levels much higher than the latest Europe assessments, but there is no evidence yet that buyers are willing to pay those prices.

Europe's dysprosium and terbium markets are in a state of flux and uncertainty. Europe does not consume a huge amount of these materials and those buyers without an urgent need may try and wait until China resumes exports before they return to the market. But that could take as long as 3-5 months if China's export controls on antimony and tungsten products offer any guide. And in the meantime, European prices are being further supported by US and Asian markets as end-users seek to buy any material they can find.

The European assessment for 99.999pc grade yttrium oxide rose to $30-46/kg cif on 1 May, compared with a fob China index of $7-7.30/kg on the same day. Bids for 5N yttrium in the mid-$40s/kg have been heard rejected in Europe since 1 May, indicating that prices continue to rise rapidly.

Yttrium metal is also soaring, pegged at around $85-150/kg cif in Europe at the start of May, compared with a fob China price of $35-38/kg.

For gadolinium, oxide offers were heard late last week in the high $300s/kg, suggesting a theoretical price level for gadolinium metal in the low $400s/kg, although no deals have been heard at these levels. In comparison, Argus' fob China assessment for min 99.999pc gadolinium oxide is at $32-34/kg and min 99pc gadolinium metal is at $44-49/kg fob China.

Not every rare earth is decoupling from China — only those affected by the export restrictions. Argus' monthly European price assessments for neodymium, cerium and erbium registered only slight movements on 1 May, still responding closely to dynamics in China, where prices have been falling owing to sluggish demand and fresh headwinds facing the magnet sector as a result of the export controls. These rare earths might decouple if exports become held up at Chinese customs along with the restricted products, but so far enough material continues to flow.

### US risk premium

US buyers are noticeably more worried than their European counterparts. China has framed the export restrictions in the context of its pre-existing ‘dual use' rules, but the timing of Beijing's announcement — two days after US president Donald Trump announced his Liberation Day reciprocal tariffs — has persuaded many market participants that the motives are political and that the US might struggle to secure export licences.

As a result, the US price rally is outpacing Europe — especially on yttrium where several market participants describe a degree of panic. Yttrium oxide traded in the US at around $100/kg in early May, while yttrium metal spot sales were heard recently at almost $200/kg.

The combination of Trump's import tariffs and China's export controls have accelerated US buyers' efforts to qualify more non-Chinese rare earth products for use in their operations, but this takes time and fundamentally there is little non-Chinese material available.

For now, it appears that US prices for the restricted rare earths are likely to rise further. Traders are unlikely to soften their offers, with one saying it makes no sense to offer below $5,000/kg for terbium oxide. And memories of the 2010 rare earths crisis — when China temporarily halted exports to Japan, sending prices soaring — loom large.

"If you're not expecting a tenfold [price] increase then you're not looking at the history properly," a market participant said.
